analysis.one_liner: Lets federal or state officials suspend all Endangered Species Act rules for federal river basins during droughts.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let the Secretary of the Army or a state governor declare that a drought threatens a region's health, safety, or welfare, and that declaration would suspend every provision of the Endangered Species Act for federal or state agencies that manage federal river basins in that region, until the drought is declared over. In practice, that means the Army Corps of Engineers and similar agencies could manage reservoirs and river flows without any of the Act's protections for endangered species and their habitats during a drought. Supporters framed it as a water-supply emergency measure; the effect is that environmental review of dam and reservoir operations would disappear exactly when water conflicts are most intense.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, cities, utilities, farms, and other water users in drought-declared regions would gain, because agencies managing federal river basins could release, store, or divert water without Endangered Species Act limits. The governor of a single affected state, acting alone, could trigger the suspension.

how_it_helps.text: The bill suspends each provision of the Endangered Species Act for any federal or state agency that manages a federal river basin once the Secretary of the Army or a state governor finds that a drought threatens the region's health, safety, or welfare. [S2] [S3]
A governor of a single state (or a designee) could make that determination without coordination with other states sharing the basin. [S3]
The suspension would end only when the same official who triggered it determines the drought is over. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Endangered species and their habitats in drought-affected basins would lose all Endangered Species Act protections for the duration of the drought, and people who value or depend on those ecosystems — including downstream users affected by changed river flows — would bear the cost. The suspension is triggered by the judgment of one official, with no defined standard for how severe a drought must be.
analysis.who_pays_short: Endangered species and downstream water users

drawbacks.text: The bill suspends the entire Act — not just the provisions that block water releases — for any agency managing a federal river basin in a drought region. [S2] [S3]
A single state's governor could trigger the suspension for a river basin that crosses into other states, whose residents, ecosystems, and industries would be affected without any say. [S3]
The bill sets no objective threshold for how severe a drought must be, leaving the suspension to one official's judgment and ending it only at that official's discretion. [S2] [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real problem — agencies balancing water supply against endangered species protections during droughts — but its remedy is sweeping: it wipes out every Endangered Species Act safeguard for federal river basins on one official's declaration, with no severity threshold, no consultation with states sharing the basin, and no limits on which provisions are suspended. A narrower fix targeting specific water-release requirements would have addressed the same conflict with far less loss of protection.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Johnny Isakson introduced the bill on October 16, 2007, with Sen. Saxby Chambliss as a cosponsor. [S1] [S3]
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works. [S5]
The bill had one cosponsor and no further recorded action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the Congress ended on January 3, 2009. [S4] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died in committee, the Endangered Species Act's protections for federal river basins during droughts remained in place — a benefit to species and habitat conservation, and to downstream interests that would have been affected by unilateral water decisions in upstream states.

for.name: Sen. Johnny Isakson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to suspend Endangered Species Act provisions for federal river basin managers during droughts.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Georgia Republicans, but no votes were ever held and no opposition was recorded, so no party-line split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill suspends every Endangered Species Act provision for federal river basin managers in a drought, removing habitat and species protections exactly when reservoir operations would most affect them. Whether the public benefits depends on how one weighs water security against species loss.

industries.industry: Municipal water utilities and other water users in drought-affected regions
industries.note: Agencies managing federal river basins could store, release, and divert water without Endangered Species Act constraints during a declared drought, easing shortages for households and businesses. This was the bill's stated purpose.

industries.industry: Downstream water-dependent interests (fisheries, coastal ecosystems, other basin states)
industries.note: Because one governor or the Army Secretary could trigger the suspension for a shared basin without consulting other states, downstream users and ecosystems would absorb the consequences of upstream water decisions made under no federal constraints.
